extracted.intended_audience: church patrons, architects, artists, clergy, and Christian stewards
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles for Christian offerings and for designing/ornamenting churches: what makes a sacrificial gift acceptable and what makes architectural decoration appropriate, honest, and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unchanging character of God vs temporary ordinances
rubrics_metrics.description: Although particular ordinances appointed for special historical purposes may be abrogated, the character of God appealed to or described in any ordinance cannot be changed by abrogation of that ordinance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle when interpreting rites: the moral/character standard behind a rite is permanent even if the external form changes; do not infer a change in divine pleasure from changes in ritual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity principle for pleasing circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain circumstances in the performance of a rite were known to please God at one time, those same circumstances will please Him at all times unless subsequently revealed otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether an element of worship remains appropriate, look for explicit revelation to the contrary; otherwise treat legitimate pleasing circumstances as enduring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptableness requires cost to the giver
rubrics_metrics.description: "Neither will I offer unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing." — Costliness (sacrifice) is a condition of acceptableness in human offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An offering that costs nothing to the giver is unacceptable; genuine sacrifice implies some personal cost or difficulty and should be expected of donors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer the best of their kind
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition of acceptableness is that offerings should be the best of their kind (the 'best of the flock'); offering inferior goods indicates a grudging or dishonoring attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donors should present the best material/skill they can afford as a testimony of respect; poor or second-rate gifts are rightly rejected as insulting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid idolatrous sympathy in splendor
rubrics_metrics.description: External splendor (purple, gold, precious materials) was not necessary to set forth God's glory and risks associating the worship of God with idolatrous forms seen elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use splendor only as a reverent sign of covenantal remembrance, not in ways that mimic pagan/idolatrous display. Be mindful of historical dangers (e.g., Israel's fall into Egyptian-like idolatry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Devote all human treasures reverently (skill, mind, materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offerings may legitimately include skill, thought, labor, artistic beauty, and the products of human industry as testimonies of love and remembrance of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden the idea of offerings beyond money — architects, artists, and patrons should render their best abilities and materials reverently to sacred service rather than hoarding them for private luxury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize essential needs over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people need walls, roofs, ministers, or basic provision, those needs take precedence over decorative expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before commissioning decorative or nonessential work, ensure fundamental needs (places to pray, ministers, teaching, charity) are met; don't let ornamentation substitute for basic ministry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute domestic luxury for church offerings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wrong to enrich one's private chambers while leaving the church bare; domestic vanities that could be offered should not be retained at the church's expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine private indulgences: a small fraction collectively offered could create substantial sacred benefit; avoid a selfish luxury that leaves the temple impoverished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts should be unostentatious and not self-proclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts may be given in an unpresuming way — small, subtle, or hidden tokens of sacrifice are morally preferable to importunate, self-proclaiming splendor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer discreet contributions (e.g., a few excellently worked shafts or capitals) over ostentatious displays intended to win admiration; place small excellences where they will be of value but not offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit of presentation matters more than outward utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptableness/usefulness of a gift is derived from the spirit in which it is presented, not from exhibition or expected reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving to gain praise or to 'purchase salvation' — offerings should be acts of heartfelt adoration, not public performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacrificial giving brings practical blessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Though not the object of giving, payment of firstfruits/tithe was historically connected with tangible rewards (wealth, length of days, peace); God does not forget works of love and multiplies what is devoutly offered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons may be encouraged that sincere sacrificial giving tends to promote increase and flourishing, and that devotion to sacred arts can revive artistic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always do your best — avoid half-work
rubrics_metrics.description: In architecture and art, it is essential that those who build or design 'do their best' and not habitually work beneath their strength or stop short wherever convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize quality over cheap completion: better to have unfinished excellent elements than completed poor ones; commission artists with the one condition they render their best work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer good lower-order work to bad higher-order work
rubrics_metrics.description: If resources are limited, choose a simpler style or rougher material but ensure it is the best of that kind rather than bad work in a higher style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the highest-quality material available within means (best brick, best Caen stone, best hatchet work) rather than attempting and failing at a grander style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive ornament — continuous work must be honest
rubrics_metrics.description: When ornament continues around a building, it is dishonest for that ornament to cease in concealed parts; hidden parts deserve honest completion or clear terminal treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either carry ornament through (even where hidden) or stop it boldly at a distinct terminal ornament so as not to deceive observers about completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute ornament according to visibility (distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicate ornaments should be placed where they are near the eye; bold and rough work should occupy parts seen from a distance so that the spectator knows what the work is and what it is worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for the viewer's vantage: reserve bas-reliefs, fine niches, and capitals for low, visible zones; use patterns and common work for distant surfaces; ensure ornament reads correctly at intended distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-delicacy and unfit detail for exposed materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that is too fine for its material or too delicate to bear exposure (e.g., ivory-like incrustation unable to withstand weather) is a serious fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the level of finish to the durability and exposure of the medium: do not cover exposed architecture with detail that cannot survive the elements — choose massy shafts and bold shadows where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must serve a true decorative/architectural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail and luxuriance are legitimate only insofar as every element has decorative power and contributes to the architectural purpose; ornament that is meaningless or mere incrustation is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ornament by its distant, decorative effect: each leaflet or figure should 'speak' and contribute to the whole; allow luxuriance only when it is honestly effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible labour: value appearance of honest work but avoid wasteful labour
rubrics_metrics.description: There is value in the appearance of labour represented by valuable materials, but the waste of actual workmanship is painful unless it is for a principle or avoids deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visible labor should not be squandered thoughtlessly; if work is 'lost' it should be in the pursuit of a legitimate principle or to avoid deception, not from lack of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place delicate work where it will be effective in mass and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicate lower work may combine with abundant upper ornament so that the upper work is effective by quantity while lower by delicacy; composition must achieve overall grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study examples (e.g., San Zeno, Rouen, Giotto's campanile) to place fine work where it enhances the mass; use quantity and intricacy aloft and delicacy near the base to obtain dignified overall effect.
